title: Palliative Sedation: Proportionate Sedation for Refractory Symptoms

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult palliative sedation for refractory symptoms in advanced terminal illness: indications, pre-sedation assessment, consent, drug selection and monitoring, using the EAPC 2009 framework.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: Only the 2009 EAPC framework was opened; the revised EAPC framework (Delphi study) and NICE NG31 sedation advice were not opened.
No Saudi guideline, Saudi legal position or religious ruling on palliative sedation was opened; local law and the hospital ethics policy apply.
The EAPC framework covers pentobarbital, not phenobarbital; pentobarbital availability in Saudi Arabia and SFDA registration of all drugs were not verified.
Doses are as printed in EAPC Appendix 2 and have not been compared with a current national formulary.
The framework gives no renal or hepatic dose adjustments.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Palliative sedation is the monitored use of medicines to induce decreased or absent awareness in order to relieve intractable suffering. A symptom is refractory when no other palliation is available within an acceptable time frame or without unacceptable adverse effects. The usual refractory symptoms are agitated delirium, dyspnoea, pain and convulsions. Catastrophic events such as massive haemorrhage, asphyxiation, severe terminal dyspnoea or an overwhelming pain crisis may need emergency sedation. Continuous deep sedation is reserved for the very terminal stage, with prognosis of hours or days at most.

symptoms: Intolerable physical distress that has not responded to other treatment.
physicalSigns: Marked restlessness or distress despite routine symptom control.
Visible respiratory distress, bleeding or seizure activity in emergencies.
redFlags: Massive haemorrhage, asphyxiation, severe terminal dyspnoea or an overwhelming pain crisis: treat as a medical emergency.

A treatable cause has not been excluded (sepsis, reversible metabolic event, medicine toxicity, pleural effusion, pericardial tamponade, ureteric or upper airway obstruction, gastrointestinal obstruction, active bleeding, urinary retention or raised intracranial pressure).
Uncertain decision-making capacity or no agreed proxy.
Refractory psychological or existential distress alone: no consensus; use only the respite-sedation approach.
precipitants: Advanced terminal illness with prognosis of hours to days.
Reversible contributors such as infection, metabolic disturbance or medicine toxicity.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: A specific cause from the exclusion list is found; treat that cause before declaring the symptom refractory.
No consensus on sedation; consider only in advanced terminal illness after repeated assessment, a multidisciplinary case conference and respite sedation for 6–24 hours first.
Signs of overdose: reduce the opioid gradually rather than stopping it abruptly.

ruleIn.expectedFinding: No further option within an acceptable time frame
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Required before sedation; a trainee's assessment must be corroborated by a senior or palliative care team.

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise refractory distress
actions: Treat extreme distress as a medical emergency and evaluate urgently.
Catastrophic events (massive haemorrhage, asphyxiation) may justify immediate deep sedation as first line.

clinicalManagement.title: Assess
actions: Experienced palliative care clinician evaluates; exclude treatable causes; review psychosocial, spiritual and environmental contributors.
Estimate prognosis and assess decision-making capacity.
Seek expert consultation if unsure that all options were tried.
Record the rationale, aims, planned depth and duration.

clinicalManagement.title: Decide and consent
actions: Discuss the cause, treatments tried, aims, depth, monitoring, expected effects and risks (paradoxical agitation, inadequate relief, possible hastened death).
Include family with the patient's permission; if capacity is absent and no advance directive exists, obtain the view of a legally recognised proxy, who states what the patient would have wanted.

Use the lowest effective level: try intermittent or mild sedation first; continuous deep sedation first line only if suffering is intense and refractory, death is expected within hours or days, the patient explicitly wishes it, or there is a catastrophic event.

clinicalManagement.title: Start and titrate
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Start with physician and nurse together
actions: Assess at least every 20 minutes until adequate sedation, then at least three times daily.
Titrate gradually to the lowest dose that relieves suffering and document each change.
In imminent death monitor comfort and respiratory rate; downward titration is generally not recommended.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing care
actions: Decide artificial hydration and nutrition separately from sedation, on the patient's wishes and comfort.
Continue symptom-relieving medicines (generally continue opioids; reduce gradually if overdose signs appear).
Keep dignified care: communication, oral, eye and skin care; support family and staff.

regimens.indication: Palliative sedation for refractory symptoms (most commonly used)
regimens.dose: Start 0.5–1 mg per hour or 1–5 mg as needed; usual effective dose 1–20 mg per hour
regimens.duration: Until sedation goal is reached and for as long as needed
adjustments: Titrate to the lowest effective dose; the source gives no renal or hepatic adjustment.
monitoring: Assess every 20 minutes until adequate sedation, then at least three times daily; RASS or comfort-based observation.
contraindications: Paradoxical agitation can occur; flumazenil reverses benzodiazepine respiratory depression in life-threatening respite sedation.

regimens.indication: Sedation when benzodiazepine and opioid tolerance is extreme (specialist)
regimens.dose: Loading 2–3 mg/kg slow IV push, no faster than 50 mg per minute; infusion 1–2 mg/kg per hour then titrate
adjustments: No analgesic effect; the source gives no renal or hepatic adjustment.
monitoring: Assess every 20 minutes until adequate sedation, then at least three times daily.
contraindications: Contraindications are not listed in the source; availability in Saudi Arabia is unverified.

medicationPlan.note: Doses are from EAPC 2009 Appendix 2 and are for adults under specialist palliative care. Midazolam and levomepromazine are the usual choices; propofol and pentobarbital are specialist options. Opioids are not appropriate sedatives. SFDA registration was not verified; check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: No other palliation available within an acceptable time frame or without unacceptable adverse effects.
Patient can express a will, understand the relevant information and understand the implications of the choice.
Assess at least every 20 minutes until adequate sedation, then at least three times daily.

teaching.scope: Adult palliative sedation for refractory symptoms in advanced terminal illness: indications, pre-sedation assessment, consent, drug selection and monitoring, using the EAPC 2009 framework.
learningObjectives: Apply proportionate, lowest-effective sedation with consent and monitoring.
pitfalls: Reducing sedation for gradual respiratory decline in imminent death.
Sedating for psychological distress without multidisciplinary review.
keyPoints: Assess at least every 20 minutes until sedated, then at least three times daily.
Hydration and nutrition are a separate decision.

patientEducation: Explain to patient (where capable) and family the aims, expected effects, risks and continued comfort care.
Explain that sedation treats suffering and that artificial hydration or nutrition is decided separately.
lifestyleAndDiet: Continue dignified care: oral, eye and skin care and a calm environment.
mdtReferrals: Specialist palliative care team; ethics advice where uncertain; psychiatry if capacity is doubtful; chaplaincy or spiritual care; nursing team for monitoring.
dischargeCriteria: Not applicable as a discharge topic; document the plan, the proxy involvement and the family discussion, and continue care in the current setting.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Document each dose change and response; revisit goals with family and team; offer bereavement support and care for staff.
